questions.q: Why do relational databases favor B-tree indexes over hash indexes for general use?
options: B-trees hash their keys internally, giving strictly faster point lookups
B-trees fit entirely in memory while hash tables must stay on disk
B-trees keep keys ordered, supporting range scans and prefix matches
B-trees never need rebalancing after inserts or deletes
questions.explanation: B-trees store keys in sorted order, so they serve ranges, prefixes, and ORDER BY as well as equality. Hash indexes only answer exact-match lookups, so they cover far fewer query shapes.

questions.q: What does a database actually do with an index during a point query like WHERE id = 42?
options: Scans the whole index sequentially, which is faster than scanning the table
Descends the tree to the key, then follows a pointer to the row
Loads the index into RAM, then binary-searches the raw table file
Rewrites the query into a join between the index and the table
questions.explanation: The engine walks from the root down a few levels to the leaf holding the key, then uses the stored row pointer to fetch the tuple. That is a handful of page reads instead of a scan.

questions.q: Adding an index to a table speeds up certain reads. What is the unavoidable cost?
options: Reads that do not use the index become slower as well
The table's rows must be physically re-sorted after every single insert
Storage doubles because the index copies every column
Every insert, update, and delete must also maintain the index
questions.explanation: An index is a second structure that must stay in sync, so every write pays extra I/O and CPU to update it. Rows are not re-sorted, and the index copies only the indexed columns.

questions.q: Which column is the worst candidate for a standalone index?
options: A boolean flag that is true for half the rows
A unique email address column used for every login lookup
A timestamp column filtered by date ranges
A foreign key column used in frequent joins
questions.explanation: A boolean matching half the table has terrible selectivity, so the index returns so many rows the planner prefers a sequential scan. Unique, range, and join columns all filter far more sharply.

questions.q: A composite index on (last_name, first_name) exists. Which query can use it efficiently?
options: WHERE first_name = 'Ana' alone, since it appears in the index
WHERE last_name = 'Silva' AND first_name > 'M'
WHERE first_name = 'Ana' OR last_name = 'Silva'
WHERE UPPER(last_name) = 'SILVA' with no expression index
questions.explanation: Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: equality on last_name pins a contiguous slice, and the range on first_name scans inside it. Filtering on first_name alone skips the leading column.

questions.q: What makes an index 'covering' for a given query?
options: It covers every row of the table, including NULL values in any column
It is declared UNIQUE, letting the planner stop at the first match
It is the clustered index, so rows and index live together on disk
It contains every column the query needs, so the table is never touched
questions.explanation: Covering means the index alone satisfies the query's column list, so the engine answers from index pages and skips the row lookups. Uniqueness and clustering are unrelated properties.

questions.q: Why does index selectivity matter to the query planner?
options: Low-selectivity indexes return so many rows that a table scan is often cheaper
Selectivity determines how many levels deep the B-tree is allowed to grow before splitting
High selectivity forces the planner to use hash joins exclusively
Selectivity controls the on-disk compression ratio of the index
questions.explanation: Each index match costs a random row fetch, so once a predicate matches a large fraction of rows, sequential scanning beats thousands of scattered lookups. Selectivity is the planner's cost signal.

questions.q: In which order do B-tree leaf pages store index entries?
options: Strict insertion order, so recently written rows always land on the rightmost page
Random order, with a hash directory mapping keys to pages
Sorted key order, with sibling links enabling in-order range scans
Physical row order, mirroring the heap file exactly
questions.explanation: Leaves hold entries sorted by key and are chained to their siblings, so a range scan finds the start key then walks the linked leaves without returning to the root.

questions.q: Why can adding five secondary indexes noticeably slow a write-heavy table?
options: Each write must update every index, multiplying random I/O per row change
The optimizer must re-plan queries after each write to a secondary index
Secondary indexes force full table locks during any insert
Each index doubles the WAL size regardless of columns touched
questions.explanation: One row change becomes six structure updates, each dirtying different pages scattered across disk. Writes do not take table locks, but the amplified random I/O dominates throughput.

questions.q: A query filters on status ('active' = 95% of rows). The planner ignores your status index. Why is that reasonable?
options: The index is likely corrupt and needs a full REINDEX before the planner trusts it
Indexes on text columns are unusable without a functional index
The planner only uses one index per table and picked the primary key
Fetching 95% of rows via the index costs more than scanning the table
questions.explanation: Reading nearly the whole table through an index means one random fetch per row plus the index pages. A sequential scan reads the same data in order, so the planner is choosing the cheaper plan.

questions.q: A query needs columns a, b, and c; you have an index on (a, b). What does adding c as an INCLUDE column achieve?
options: It lets the index enforce a uniqueness constraint spanning all three columns together
It makes the index covering, eliminating per-row heap or clustered-index lookups
It reorders the index to (a, b, c), speeding range scans on c
It compresses the index by deduplicating repeated values of c
questions.explanation: INCLUDE stores c as payload in the leaf pages without adding it to the key, so the query is answered entirely from the index. Because c is not a key column, it cannot be searched or affect uniqueness.

questions.q: Why might a range query on the second column of a composite index (a, b) perform poorly?
options: Composite indexes physically store only the first column's values inside their leaf pages
Range predicates are illegal on any column after the first
Without an equality filter on a, matching b values are scattered across the index
The second column is stored unsorted to save page space
questions.explanation: The index is sorted by a first, so b is only ordered within each a group. Skipping a predicate on a leaves matching b values spread over the whole index, forcing a full index scan.

questions.q: Bulk-loading 100M rows into a table with six indexes is crawling. Common mitigation?
options: Raise the transaction isolation level so the loader takes fewer row locks overall
Shrink the B-tree fill factor to zero so pages never split
Switch the table to a hash index during the load window
Drop or disable the indexes, load the data, then rebuild them once
questions.explanation: Maintaining six trees per row is the bottleneck. Building each index once from sorted data afterward is a bulk sequential operation, far cheaper than 600M incremental updates.

questions.q: An index on created_at exists, but WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-08-16' scans the table. Why?
options: Wrapping the column in a function hides it from the index unless an expression index exists
DATE() returns a string, and string comparisons cannot use B-trees
Timestamps are stored as integers, so date filters require a cast scan
The index only covers rows created after it was built
questions.explanation: The index stores raw created_at values, not DATE(created_at), so the predicate is non-sargable. Rewriting it as a half-open range, or indexing the expression, restores index use.

questions.q: What is write amplification in the context of an LSM-tree storage engine?
options: Writes amplify read latency by evicting hot pages out of the shared buffer pool
The WAL records each write twice, once per replica, doubling disk traffic
One logical write is rewritten multiple times as compaction merges levels
Deletes expand into tombstones larger than the original values
questions.explanation: A key written once is copied again each time compaction merges it into a deeper level, so bytes written to disk far exceed bytes the application wrote.

questions.q: When is a partial (filtered) index the right tool?
options: When the table is small enough that any index fits in a single page
When queries target a small, well-defined slice, like unshipped orders
When you need to index every column but storage is limited
When the optimizer refuses hints and you must force index usage
questions.explanation: Indexing only the rows matching a WHERE clause keeps the structure tiny and cheap to maintain, which pays off when hot queries always target that same narrow, predictable subset.

questions.q: A UUIDv4 primary key on a clustered-index engine (InnoDB) causes heavy write degradation at scale. Root cause?
options: UUID comparisons are lexicographic, so each lookup descends twice as many tree levels
Random key order scatters inserts across pages, causing splits and cache misses
UUIDs exceed the 8-byte key limit, forcing overflow pages per row
The engine hashes UUIDs before storing, adding CPU per insert
questions.explanation: Random keys land in arbitrary leaf pages, so the working set is the whole index rather than a hot right edge, producing page splits, fragmentation, and buffer-pool misses. Sortable UUIDv7 or ULIDs fix this.

questions.q: Index-only scans sometimes still hit the heap in Postgres. Why?
options: The planner always verifies 10% of rows against the heap for safety
Covering indexes exclude NULLs, so NULL rows require heap access
Pages not marked all-visible force heap checks to confirm tuple visibility
TOASTed column values always live in the heap even when the index covers that column
questions.explanation: Postgres index entries carry no MVCC visibility info, so unless the visibility map marks a heap page all-visible, the tuple must be checked. Keeping autovacuum current maximizes true index-only scans.

questions.q: You must support queries filtering on any 2 of 8 columns. Indexing every 2-column combination is infeasible. Reasonable approach?
options: Index each column singly and let the planner combine them with bitmap AND
Create a single eight-column composite index ordered by descending column popularity
Use a hash index per column pair, since hash indexes are tiny
Add a trigger that builds temporary indexes per incoming query
questions.explanation: Eight single-column indexes cover all 28 pairs: the planner builds a bitmap from each relevant index and ANDs them before touching the heap. A wide composite index only helps its leftmost prefixes.

questions.q: A 500 GB table gets a new index; the build locks writes for hours. What do modern databases offer to avoid this?
options: Building the index purely in memory and persisting it at the next restart
Indexing a 1% sample of rows and backfilling the remainder lazily on access
Queueing all writes in the WAL until the build completes, then replaying them
An online build that tracks concurrent table changes and applies them at the end
questions.explanation: Concurrent builds (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, ALGORITHM=INPLACE) scan the table while logging concurrent DML, then replay that log to catch up, so writes keep flowing at the cost of a slower build.
